svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 3. Draw your recovery graph, and look for the loop
svg.desc: Two diagrams of recovery dependencies. The first shows the loop that standard advice produces: the email account is recovered by its recovery codes, those codes are stored in the password vault, and the vault is recovered through the email account. Every node depends on another node in the circle, so losing any one of them loses all three. The second shows an acyclic arrangement in which the email account and the vault both terminate at a physical store holding a second hardware key, printed codes and a vault backup, which depends on nothing that can be lost online and on nobody who can be talked past. A band below states the rule that every recovery graph needs a root that depends on nothing else, and that the root must be physical.
svg.text: Figure 3: Draw the Graph, and Look for the Loop
Standard advice produces the diagram on the left. It gives sound instructions one at a time and never draws them together.
THE LOOP MOST PEOPLE HAVE
every arrow reads "is recovered by" or "is kept in"
Your email account
Its recovery codes
issued once, at setup
Your password vault
where you were told to put them
recovered by
kept in
recovered by
Three nodes, three arrows, no way out.
Lose any one of them and you have lost all three.
THE GRAPH YOU WANT
the same arrows, arranged so the chain terminates
Your email account
Your password vault
both recovered by
A physical store you control
A second hardware key, the codes on paper, and a copy of the vault.
A safe, a deposit box, or a locked drawer somewhere else.
This node has no outgoing arrow, which is the entire point.
It cannot be phished, reset by a support agent, or lost with a device.
The rule, which takes ten minutes to check and is almost never checked
Every recovery graph needs at least one root: a node that depends on nothing else. If no node qualifies, you have a loop rather than a plan.

g.text: The root has to be physical. Anything online is recoverable by somebody, which means it has an incoming arrow you did not draw and did not choose.
Each instruction on the left is individually correct. Store codes in the vault. Secure the vault with the email. The loop only appears when you draw them together.

svg.text: Do this on paper for your own accounts before the lab asks you to. It takes one sheet, and most people find the loop within about five minutes.
A local vault with no online recovery does not escape this. It makes the vault the root, so the paper copy in the safe is the only thing standing behind everything.
The failure this prevents is not a compromise. It is the quieter one where nothing was attacked and you simply cannot get in.
